notes: PART 2 of 2 — culture, language, food, festival and memory tracks of the Louisiana OS (part 1 carries river, coast, energy, ports, agriculture). Same pack name; generate_pack.py is run on both parts and the normalizer merges rows under one pack. Cultural facts are public record; checks are phrased against the learner's own parish and elders so they stay true statewide.

themes.description: The roux as the foundation — flour, fat, patience — and the colors that decide what dish it becomes.
themes.transfer_check: Make a roux to a stated color without burning it, and say which dish each of three colors belongs to.

bands.K–2: Watch an adult stir a roux, smell it change, and say which colour it is now.
bands.3–5: Stir a roux with an adult to a light colour without burning it, and say which dish it is for.
bands.6–8: Make a roux to a stated colour with a checker at the stove, and say which dish two of the three colours belong to.
bands.9–10: Make a roux to a stated color without burning it, and say which dish each of three colors belongs to.
bands.11–12: Make three roux to three colours in one session, teach the stir to a younger learner, and cook one dish on the darkest.

themes.description: Onion, celery, bell pepper — the base of the cuisine, and the pot cookery built on it.
themes.transfer_check: Prepare the trinity correctly and build one real pot dish on it, narrating what each stage contributes.

bands.K–2: Help wash and count the onion, celery and bell pepper, and name them as the trinity.
bands.3–5: Chop the trinity with an adult and start one pot dish on it, saying what each vegetable adds.
bands.6–8: Prepare the trinity correctly with a checker and build one pot dish on it, narrating two of the stages.
bands.9–10: Prepare the trinity correctly and build one real pot dish on it, narrating what each stage contributes.
bands.11–12: Prepare the trinity and cook two different pot dishes on it for a group, explaining at the table what the base does in each.

themes.description: Okra, filé, roux — the gumbo lineages, why no two families agree, and the respect owed to each version.
themes.transfer_check: Cook one gumbo in a named lineage and document a second household's differing version without ruling either wrong.

bands.K–2: Taste gumbo from two households and say one thing that was different, and that both are right.
bands.3–5: Ask two families how they make gumbo and write down one difference without saying whose is better.
bands.6–8: Cook one gumbo in a named lineage with a checker, and document one difference in another household's version without ruling it wrong.
bands.9–10: Cook one gumbo in a named lineage and document a second household's differing version without ruling either wrong.
bands.11–12: Cook a gumbo for a group, document two other households' versions with their keepers, and present the lineages with respect for each.

themes.theme: The boil as a public event
themes.description: Crawfish and shrimp boils — the seasoning, the timing, the table covered in newspaper — cooking as gathering.
themes.transfer_check: Plan and run (or fully rehearse) a boil for a real group — quantities, seasoning, timing, safe handling — through to the table.

bands.K–2: Help lay the newspaper and count the plates for a family boil, and learn the hot-pot rule.
bands.3–5: Help plan a small boil — how many, how much, when it goes in — and help serve it safely.
bands.6–8: Plan and help run a boil for a small group with a checker on the seasoning, timing and safe handling.
bands.9–10: Plan and run (or fully rehearse) a boil for a real group — quantities, seasoning, timing, safe handling — through to the table.
bands.11–12: Plan and run a boil for a real community group, do the batch maths and the safety plan, and account for what it cost and raised.

themes.description: The sausage craft of the prairies and the German Coast — what goes in, how it is smoked, and where to find the real thing.
themes.transfer_check: Make or closely document one batch of boudin or andouille at a real kitchen or shop, recording the method start to finish.

bands.K–2: Visit a boudin shop or smokehouse with an adult, taste, and say what is inside.
bands.3–5: Watch or study how boudin is made and draw the steps from meat and rice to the link.
bands.6–8: Closely document one batch of boudin or andouille at a real kitchen or shop, recording the method start to finish.
bands.9–10: Make or closely document one batch of boudin or andouille at a real kitchen or shop, recording the method start to finish.
bands.11–12: Make a batch under a maker's eye, document the method for a stranger, and compare two shops' methods with their makers' consent.

themes.theme: Cajun and Creole are not the same word
themes.description: Two cuisines with tangled roots — country and city, prairie and port — told through their dishes and histories.
themes.transfer_check: Present one dish in its Cajun and its Creole expression, explaining the historical reason for each difference, with sources.

bands.K–2: Learn that Cajun and Creole are two different ways of cooking and living, and taste one dish from each.
bands.3–5: Say one thing that is Cajun and one thing that is Creole about the same dish, with an adult's help.
bands.6–8: Present one dish in its Cajun and its Creole expression and explain one historical reason for the difference, with a source.
bands.9–10: Present one dish in its Cajun and its Creole expression, explaining the historical reason for each difference, with sources.
bands.11–12: Present two dishes both ways with sources, and lead a class discussion that keeps the two words honest and respectful.

themes.description: Shrimp, oysters, catfish and the gulf catch — buying Louisiana seafood knowledgeably and handling it safely.
themes.transfer_check: At a real counter or dock, identify the local catch, judge its freshness, and prepare one item with correct safe handling.

bands.K–2: Go to a seafood counter or dock with an adult and name three things from Louisiana water.
bands.3–5: At a counter, say how you can tell if fish and shrimp are fresh, and help prepare one safely at home.

bands.9–10: At a real counter or dock, identify the local catch, judge its freshness, and prepare one item with correct safe handling.
bands.11–12: Buy, judge and prepare three local items for a group, and teach the freshness and safety checks to a younger learner.

themes.description: Why rice anchors the plate — from the fields of the prairie to jambalaya, étouffée and red beans on Monday.

bands.K–2: Help measure rice and water for the family pot, and learn why Monday is red beans day.
bands.3–5: Cook a pot of rice with an adult and serve it under one dish, telling the Monday red beans story.
bands.6–8: Cook rice properly for a family with a checker and serve it under one classic preparation, explaining the Monday tradition.
bands.9–10: Cook rice properly at scale and serve it under one classic preparation, explaining the Monday red beans tradition while it simmers.
bands.11–12: Cook rice at scale for a community feed under two preparations, and explain the rice-and-Monday tradition to the table.

themes.description: Documenting family foodways — the pinch and the handful written down before they are lost.
themes.transfer_check: Record one real family or community recipe from its keeper — quantities, technique, story — into a form a stranger could cook from.

bands.K–2: Ask an elder how they make one dish and draw the steps.
bands.3–5: Write down one family recipe from its keeper — what goes in, how much, the story — and cook it with them.
bands.6–8: Record one family or community recipe from its keeper — quantities, technique, story — into a form a friend could cook from.
bands.9–10: Record one real family or community recipe from its keeper — quantities, technique, story — into a form a stranger could cook from.
bands.11–12: Record two recipes from two keepers with consent, cook one for them, and archive both where the family can reach them.

themes.description: The capstone: church suppers, benefit plate lunches and disaster kitchens — Louisiana cooking as civic infrastructure.
themes.transfer_check: Help run or fully plan one real community feed — the plates, the batch math, the safe service — and account for what it raised or delivered.

bands.K–2: Help at a church supper or a class feed — carry, serve, tidy — and say who it was for.
bands.3–5: Help plan a small community feed — how many plates, what goes on each — and help serve it.
bands.6–8: Help run one real community feed — the plates, the batch maths, the safe service — with a checker on the numbers.
bands.9–10: Help run or fully plan one real community feed — the plates, the batch math, the safe service — and account for what it raised or delivered.
bands.11–12: Plan and run a real community feed end to end, account for it, and hand the plan to the next crew.

tracks.name: Music: the sound the state gave the world

themes.theme: Congo Square and the root of it
themes.description: The Sunday gatherings in New Orleans where African rhythm kept its public voice — and what grew from that ground.
themes.transfer_check: Present the documented history of Congo Square and trace one musical line from it to a form you can play or play back.

bands.3–5: Tell the story of Congo Square in your own words and clap one rhythm that grew from it.

bands.9–10: Present the documented history of Congo Square and trace one musical line from it to a form you can play or play back.
bands.11–12: Present the history with sources, trace two lines from it, and teach the root rhythm to a younger group.

themes.description: Collective improvisation, the second line beat and the horns — how New Orleans assembled jazz from its neighborhoods.
themes.transfer_check: Identify the parts of one early New Orleans jazz recording by ear — lead, harmony, rhythm — and clap or play its second-line figure.

bands.3–5: Listen to an early New Orleans jazz recording and say which instrument leads and which keeps time, and clap the beat.
bands.6–8: Identify the parts of one early New Orleans jazz recording by ear — lead, harmony, rhythm — and clap its second-line figure.
bands.9–10: Identify the parts of one early New Orleans jazz recording by ear — lead, harmony, rhythm — and clap or play its second-line figure.
bands.11–12: Identify the parts on two recordings, play the second-line figure with others, and present how the neighbourhoods assembled the music.

themes.theme: The brass band and the street
themes.description: Parade bands from funeral dirge to street celebration — the repertoire, the instrumentation, the roles.
themes.transfer_check: March or perform one piece in a brass-band arrangement, holding your part, or direct a recorded analysis of a real parade performance.

bands.K–2: March in a line to a brass band recording, playing or pretending an instrument, and learn what a second line is.
bands.3–5: Play or clap one part of a brass-band piece with the class, holding your part.
bands.6–8: Perform one piece in a brass-band arrangement in a group, holding your part, or analyse a recorded parade performance with a checker.
bands.9–10: March or perform one piece in a brass-band arrangement, holding your part, or direct a recorded analysis of a real parade performance.
bands.11–12: Lead or arrange a brass-band piece for a group, march it, and teach the roles to younger players.

themes.description: Accordion, rubboard and the southwest Louisiana Saturday night — zydeco's Creole roots and living circuit.
themes.transfer_check: Learn zydeco's basic rhythm on any instrument or rubboard and identify two living artists on the real regional circuit.

bands.K–2: Hear zydeco, find the rubboard sound, and scrape a rhythm on a board or a washboard.
bands.3–5: Learn zydeco's basic rhythm on a rubboard or any instrument and name one zydeco artist.
bands.6–8: Learn zydeco's basic rhythm on any instrument or rubboard and identify one living artist on the regional circuit.
bands.9–10: Learn zydeco's basic rhythm on any instrument or rubboard and identify two living artists on the real regional circuit.
bands.11–12: Play the rhythm with others at tempo, attend or document a dancehall night, and present the living circuit to a class.

themes.theme: Cajun music: the ballads of the prairie
themes.description: Fiddle, accordion and French singing — the Cajun repertoire and the dance halls that keep it working music.
themes.transfer_check: Perform or accompany one Cajun standard, or document a real dance-hall night — the band, the steps, the sung French.

bands.K–2: Hear a Cajun waltz, learn one French word from it, and sway in time.
bands.3–5: Sing or play along with one Cajun song and learn what the dance halls are.
bands.6–8: Accompany one Cajun standard on any instrument with a checker, or document a dance-hall night — the band, the steps.
bands.9–10: Perform or accompany one Cajun standard, or document a real dance-hall night — the band, the steps, the sung French.
bands.11–12: Perform a Cajun standard for a real audience and document a dance-hall night with its musicians' consent.

themes.description: The choirs and quartets — gospel as the training ground of Louisiana voices, sacred music as community practice.
themes.transfer_check: Sing in or closely document one real choir or quartet rehearsal, mapping the parts and the call-and-response at work.

bands.K–2: Sing in a group call-and-response song and learn that many singers started in church.
bands.3–5: Listen to a gospel choir and say which voices sing which parts, and join a group song.
bands.6–8: Sing in or closely document one choir or quartet rehearsal, mapping the parts with a checker.
bands.9–10: Sing in or closely document one real choir or quartet rehearsal, mapping the parts and the call-and-response at work.
bands.11–12: Sing in a rehearsal and lead a call-and-response with the group, or document a rehearsal and present its method to a class.

themes.theme: The blues highway through the north
themes.description: North Louisiana's blues and its highways — the juke joints, the labels, the artists who carried it out.
themes.transfer_check: Profile one documented north Louisiana blues artist and learn a twelve-bar form well enough to play or analyze their recording.

bands.K–2: Hear a north Louisiana blues song and clap along on the beat.
bands.3–5: Learn the twelve-bar blues shape by counting bars along with a recording, and name one artist from north Louisiana.
bands.6–8: Profile one documented north Louisiana blues artist and learn a twelve-bar form well enough to count and clap through their recording.
bands.9–10: Profile one documented north Louisiana blues artist and learn a twelve-bar form well enough to play or analyze their recording.
bands.11–12: Profile the artist, play the twelve-bar form with others, and present the highway, the labels and the artists as one story.

themes.description: From Cosimo's rooms to the streaming ledger — how Louisiana records got made and who got paid, then and now.
themes.transfer_check: Trace one classic Louisiana recording's business story — studio, label, songwriter credit — and compare it to a streaming payout today.

bands.K–2: Learn that a song is made in a studio and that the people who make it are supposed to get paid.
bands.3–5: Find one classic Louisiana recording and say who wrote it and where it was recorded.
bands.6–8: Trace one classic Louisiana recording's business story — studio, label, songwriter credit — from documented sources.
bands.9–10: Trace one classic Louisiana recording's business story — studio, label, songwriter credit — and compare it to a streaming payout today.
bands.11–12: Trace two recordings' business stories, compute what each would earn on streaming today, and present who got paid then and now.

themes.description: The working musician's Louisiana — gigs, festivals, sideman work and the arithmetic of a music year.
themes.transfer_check: Interview or study one real working Louisiana musician and chart their actual year — gigs, income streams, the hardest month.

bands.K–2: Meet or hear about a working musician and name three places they play.
bands.3–5: Interview a musician about their year — where they play, how they get paid.
bands.6–8: Study one real working Louisiana musician and chart their year — gigs, income streams — from an interview or their own account.
bands.9–10: Interview or study one real working Louisiana musician and chart their actual year — gigs, income streams, the hardest month.
bands.11–12: Interview two musicians, chart both years, and present the arithmetic of a music year to a class thinking of the life.

themes.description: The capstone: the tradition's transmission — school bands, church, family — and taking your own place in it.
themes.transfer_check: Prepare and give one real performance in any Louisiana tradition, and teach its basic figure to a younger learner.

bands.K–2: Play or sing one Louisiana tune for the class and show a friend the first note.
bands.3–5: Give one small performance in a Louisiana tradition and teach a younger child its rhythm.
bands.6–8: Prepare and give one performance in any Louisiana tradition for a class, and teach its basic figure to a younger learner.
bands.9–10: Prepare and give one real performance in any Louisiana tradition, and teach its basic figure to a younger learner.
bands.11–12: Give a real performance for a public audience and take a younger learner through a full piece to their own performance.

tracks.name: French, Creole and the languages of home

themes.description: Louisiana French, Kouri-Vini (Louisiana Creole), Spanish, Vietnamese and the rest — the state's language map and the histories under it.
themes.transfer_check: Map the languages historically and currently spoken in your own parish, with one documented source per language.

bands.K–2: Learn the names of two languages spoken in Louisiana besides English and say hello in one.
bands.3–5: Map the languages spoken in your parish now and long ago, with help from a book or a website.
bands.6–8: Map the languages historically and currently spoken in your parish, with one source for two of them.
bands.9–10: Map the languages historically and currently spoken in your own parish, with one documented source per language.
bands.11–12: Map the languages with sources, interview one speaker of a heritage language, and present the map with the histories under it.

themes.description: When French was punished in schools — the generation that stopped speaking, told from documented accounts.

bands.K–2: Hear the story of children who were told not to speak French at school, and say how that would feel.

themes.description: Louisiana French and Kouri-Vini side by side — what distinguishes them, and why the difference deserves respect.
themes.transfer_check: From recordings, distinguish Louisiana French from Kouri-Vini on three features, and say each variety's name correctly.

bands.3–5: Listen to recordings of Louisiana French and Kouri-Vini and say one way they sound different.
bands.6–8: From recordings, distinguish Louisiana French from Kouri-Vini on two features, and say each variety's name correctly.
bands.9–10: From recordings, distinguish Louisiana French from Kouri-Vini on three features, and say each variety's name correctly.
bands.11–12: Distinguish the two on three features with examples, and present to a class why the difference deserves respect, with a speaker's words.

themes.description: A working vocabulary — greetings, kitchen, weather, kin — in Louisiana French or Kouri-Vini, learned aloud.
themes.transfer_check: Hold a one-minute exchange — greeting, three questions, farewell — in Louisiana French or Kouri-Vini with a speaker or teacher.

bands.K–2: Learn ten words in Louisiana French or Kouri-Vini — hello, thank you, the kitchen — and say them aloud.
bands.3–5: Learn thirty words of home in Louisiana French or Kouri-Vini and use them in a short exchange with a speaker or teacher.
bands.6–8: Hold a short exchange — greeting, two questions, farewell — in Louisiana French or Kouri-Vini with a speaker or teacher.
bands.9–10: Hold a one-minute exchange — greeting, three questions, farewell — in Louisiana French or Kouri-Vini with a speaker or teacher.
bands.11–12: Hold a three-minute exchange with a speaker, and teach twenty words of home to a younger learner until they can greet and ask.

themes.description: Language living in food, music and prayer — learning through the domains where it never fully left.
themes.transfer_check: Collect ten living heritage-language terms from a real kitchen, song or blessing in your region, with meanings from a speaker.

bands.K–2: Learn three heritage-language words from a kitchen, a song or a blessing at home.
bands.3–5: Collect five heritage-language words from a real kitchen, song or blessing, with what they mean from a speaker.
bands.6–8: Collect ten living heritage-language terms from a real kitchen, song or blessing in your region, checking meanings with a speaker.
bands.9–10: Collect ten living heritage-language terms from a real kitchen, song or blessing in your region, with meanings from a speaker.
bands.11–12: Collect twenty terms across two domains from two speakers, and make the illustrated card set a family could use at the table.

themes.description: French immersion in Louisiana public schools and CODOFIL's work — how the revival actually runs.

bands.K–2: Learn that some Louisiana schools teach in French all day, and say one thing you would like about that.
bands.3–5: Find the nearest French immersion school and say what grades it has.
bands.6–8: Profile the nearest real immersion program — where, what grades, how to enrol — and study one family's experience of it.
bands.9–10: Profile the nearest real immersion program — where, what grades, how enrolled — and interview or study one family's experience of it.
bands.11–12: Profile the program, interview a family and a teacher, and present how the revival actually runs, with CODOFIL's own figures.

themes.description: Recording speakers properly — consent, equipment, transcription — so a voice outlives its speaker.
themes.transfer_check: Record one heritage-language speaker with consent, transcribe two minutes, and archive the recording where family can reach it.

bands.K–2: Listen to a recording of an elder speaking the old language and say one word you heard.
bands.3–5: Record an elder saying a few phrases, with their yes, and play it back to them.
bands.6–8: Record one heritage-language speaker with consent, transcribe one minute, and keep the recording where the family can reach it.
bands.9–10: Record one heritage-language speaker with consent, transcribe two minutes, and archive the recording where family can reach it.
bands.11–12: Record two speakers with consent, transcribe and translate a passage from each, and archive both with a community institution.

themes.description: Vietnamese on the coast, Spanish across the state, and the newest arrivals — the language map still being drawn.
themes.transfer_check: Document one newer language community in Louisiana — where it settled, why, what it built — from its own institutions.

bands.K–2: Learn that new families bring new languages to Louisiana, and say hello in one of them.
bands.3–5: Find one newer language community in Louisiana and say where it lives and one thing it built.
bands.6–8: Document one newer language community in Louisiana — where it settled, why, what it built — from one of its own institutions.
bands.9–10: Document one newer language community in Louisiana — where it settled, why, what it built — from its own institutions.
bands.11–12: Document the community from its institutions and an interview, and present it to a class as part of the state's language map.

themes.description: The public face of revival — bilingual signage, French media, festival stages — and what visibility does for a language.
themes.transfer_check: Inventory the real public presence of French or Creole in one town — signs, radio, mass, stage — and propose one addition to it.

bands.K–2: Find a French word on a sign, a menu or a street name in your town and say what it means.
bands.3–5: Make a list of where French or Creole shows up in public in your town — signs, radio, church, a festival.
bands.6–8: Inventory the public presence of French or Creole in one town — signs, radio, mass, stage — and propose one addition.
bands.9–10: Inventory the real public presence of French or Creole in one town — signs, radio, mass, stage — and propose one addition to it.
bands.11–12: Inventory the presence, propose the addition to the body that could make it, and record the response.

themes.theme: Keeping it alive in your house
themes.description: The capstone: a household language practice — small, daily, sustainable — designed and actually begun.
themes.transfer_check: Design and run two weeks of a real household heritage-language practice — the daily moment, the phrases — and report what stuck.

bands.K–2: Say one heritage-language phrase at the table every day for a week.
bands.3–5: Design one daily language moment for your house — a greeting, a blessing, a song — and do it for a week.
bands.6–8: Design and run one week of a real household heritage-language practice — the daily moment, the phrases — and report what stuck.
bands.9–10: Design and run two weeks of a real household heritage-language practice — the daily moment, the phrases — and report what stuck.
bands.11–12: Design and run a month of household practice, involve every member, and write the plan another household could start tomorrow.

tracks.name: Krewes, festivals and the craft of celebration

themes.description: Behind the parade — dues, committees, captains and a year of work for a night of joy; the krewe as civic machinery.

bands.K–2: Learn that a parade takes a whole year of work by a club, and name one job in it.
bands.3–5: Profile one krewe or parading club — its name, when it parades, what it does all year.
bands.6–8: Profile one real krewe or parading club — its structure and calendar — from its own materials.
bands.9–10: Profile one real krewe or parading club — its structure, calendar and budget scale — from its own materials or members.
bands.11–12: Profile the krewe from its members, and present it to a class as civic machinery with the year's calendar and money.

themes.description: Twelfth Night to Fat Tuesday — the season's actual structure, and why the date moves.
themes.transfer_check: Compute Mardi Gras's date for three different years and lay out one real community's carnival calendar across a season.

bands.K–2: Learn that Mardi Gras moves each year and find this year's date on the calendar.
bands.3–5: Work out Mardi Gras's date for next year from Easter and mark the season on a calendar.
bands.6–8: Compute Mardi Gras's date for two years and lay out one community's carnival calendar across a season.

bands.3–5: Build a small float element with a structure that holds and a finish that lasts a day.
bands.6–8: Build one small float or prop element with sound structure and finish, or document a float barn's build with a checker.

bands.11–12: Build a float element to a barn's standard, or document a full build with the artists, and present the trade to a class.

bands.9–10: Complete one real costume or beadwork piece to wearable standard, or closely document a suit's making with its maker's consent.

bands.3–5: Plan a small school parade — route, order, safety, cleanup — on one page.
bands.6–8: Produce the logistics plan for a modeled small parade — route, permits, order, safety, cleanup — with a checker.
bands.9–10: Produce the full logistics plan for a real or modeled small parade — route, permits, order, safety, cleanup — to a standard an official could approve.
bands.11–12: Produce the plan for a real parade, present it to the official who approves such plans, and revise it from their notes.

themes.description: From Jazz Fest to the smallest church fair — what festivals earn, who they pay, and the volunteer hours underneath.

bands.3–5: For one festival, find how many people come and one way it makes money.
bands.6–8: For one real Louisiana festival, chart attendance and economics from published figures, and shadow one shift.
